title: Google Ads for Service Businesses: A Practical Guide | RevUp
description: How US service businesses can use Google Ads and Local Services Ads to get more calls and booked jobs: campaign types, keywords, targeting, tracking and common mistakes.
h1: Google Ads for service businesses: a practical guide to more calls and booked jobs
excerpt: The campaign types, keywords, targeting and tracking that help plumbers, contractors, clinics and other service businesses turn Google searches into booked jobs.

sections.h2: Why Google Ads fits service businesses so well
paragraphs: Most service jobs start with a search. When a water heater fails, a tooth hurts or a roof leaks, people don't scroll social media looking for inspiration — they open Google, type what they need and call one of the first businesses they trust. That intent is what makes Google Ads so powerful for service businesses: you're paying to appear in front of people who already need what you do.
The flip side is that Google Ads can also waste money quickly if it isn't set up for how service businesses actually get customers. This guide covers the decisions that matter most.

sections.h2: Choose the right campaign type
paragraphs: For most service businesses, the core is a Google Search campaign: text ads that appear when someone searches for your service in your area. Search gives you control over keywords, ad copy, landing pages and budget by service.

In the United States, many service categories are also eligible for Local Services Ads. These appear above the regular ads, show your reviews and verification badges, and charge per lead instead of per click. They're worth testing if your category is eligible, but you have less control over how leads are matched, so many businesses run them alongside Search rather than instead of it.

Performance Max can work for some service businesses, but it optimizes toward whatever conversions you give it. If your tracking counts low-quality form fills or short calls as conversions, it can bring volume without real jobs. Get your tracking right first.

sections.h2: Pick keywords that bring buyers, not researchers
paragraphs: Focus on searches that show someone is ready to hire: the service plus a location ("ac repair miami"), "near me" searches and urgent phrases like "emergency plumber" or "same day". Organize campaigns by service, so each service has its own ads and its own landing page.
Just as important are negative keywords — searches you don't want to pay for. Common ones for service businesses include:
bullets: Job seekers: "jobs", "salary", "hiring", "training"
Do-it-yourselfers: "how to", "diy", "youtube", "parts"
Bargain hunters you can't serve profitably: "free", "cheapest"
Services you don't offer and areas you don't cover

sections.h2: Target your real service area and hours
paragraphs: Set your locations to the cities, ZIP codes or radius you actually serve, and use the location option that targets people who are in or regularly in those areas — not people merely interested in them. A lead from outside your service area is a wasted click.
Schedule your ads for the hours someone can answer the phone. If calls go to voicemail at night, either lower bids during those hours or send those clicks to a page with a strong booking form.

sections.h2: Write ads that earn the call
paragraphs: Service customers want to know three things fast: can you do this job, can you do it soon, and can they trust you. Put the service and city in the headline, mention speed or availability if it's true, and add real trust signals like years in business, licensing or your review rating.

Use assets to take up more space and make calling easier: call assets so mobile users can tap to call, location assets linked to your Google Business Profile, and sitelinks to your most important services.

sections.h2: Send clicks to a page built for that service
paragraphs: Sending every ad to your homepage is one of the most expensive mistakes. Each service should have a landing page that matches the ad, loads fast on a phone, shows a clickable phone number at the top, uses a short form and includes proof: reviews, photos of real jobs and the areas you serve.

sections.h2: Track calls and booked jobs, not clicks
paragraphs: Clicks don't pay the bills — jobs do. At minimum, track calls from your ads, calls from your website and form submissions as separate conversions. Better still, record which leads became booked jobs and send that back to Google, so bidding learns to find more people like your best customers.
With good tracking you can answer the questions that matter: what does a lead cost for each service, what does a booked job cost and which campaigns are profitable.

sections.h2: Common Google Ads mistakes service businesses make
paragraphs: Most wasted budget we see comes from the same handful of issues:
bullets: Broad keywords with no negative keyword list
Targeting people "interested in" your area instead of people in it
One campaign for every service, sending traffic to the homepage
Counting page views or short calls as conversions
Changing everything every few days before the data can mean anything

sections.h2: Where to start
paragraphs: Start with your most profitable service in your core area, a dedicated landing page and proper call and form tracking. Give the campaign a few weeks to collect data, clean up search terms weekly and expand to more services and cities once the numbers work. title: Facebook & Instagram Ads for Service Businesses | RevUp
description: How US service businesses can generate quality leads with Facebook and Instagram ads: offers, lead forms, WhatsApp campaigns, creative, targeting and fast follow-up.
h1: How service businesses get quality leads from Facebook & Instagram ads
excerpt: Offers, lead forms, WhatsApp campaigns and creative that help contractors, clinics and local service businesses turn social media attention into booked appointments.

sections.h2: Social ads create demand — Google captures it
paragraphs: Google Ads reaches people already searching for your service. Facebook and Instagram work differently: you reach people before they search, while they're scrolling. For a service business, that means Meta ads are best at creating demand — getting homeowners to book the AC tune-up before summer, patients to schedule the consultation they've been postponing, or property owners to request a quote.
Because people weren't looking for you, your offer and creative have to do the work. Here's what makes the difference.

sections.h2: Lead with a clear, low-risk offer
paragraphs: "We do great work" isn't an offer. Give people a specific, low-risk reason to raise their hand now. Offers that tend to work well for service businesses include:
bullets: Free estimate, inspection or consultation
Seasonal services with a clear deadline (tune-ups, gutter cleaning, pre-summer checkups)
A first-visit or new-customer package with a transparent price
Financing or payment plans for bigger jobs

sections.h2: Choose the right way to capture the lead
paragraphs: Meta instant forms let people submit their details without leaving the app. They usually produce the most leads at the lowest cost, but quality can be lower. Adding a few qualifying questions — service needed, ZIP code, timeline — or using the higher-intent form option filters out people who aren't serious.
Sending people to a landing page brings fewer but often better-qualified leads, and works well when you need to explain the service or show reviews first.

Click-to-message campaigns open a conversation on WhatsApp or Messenger. For many service businesses, especially in bilingual markets, a chat feels easier than a form, and your team can qualify and book the customer in the same conversation.

sections.h2: Use creative that looks real
paragraphs: The ads that work for service businesses rarely look like polished commercials. They show your actual team, trucks, clinic or projects. Some formats that consistently earn attention:
bullets: Before-and-after photos of real jobs
Short videos of the owner or a technician explaining the offer
Real customer reviews, shown with permission
Simple, direct text: the service, the area and the offer

sections.h2: Target your service area and let the data work
paragraphs: Set a location radius around the areas you serve and keep targeting fairly broad inside it — Meta's algorithm is good at finding people likely to respond once it has conversion data. Add retargeting for people who visited your website or engaged with your ads, and exclude existing customers when you're promoting new-customer offers.

sections.h2: Speed to lead makes or breaks your results
paragraphs: A lead from social media is warm for minutes, not days. Many prospects submit forms to several businesses, and the first one to call often wins the job. Set up instant notifications for every new lead, call within minutes during business hours and use an automatic WhatsApp or text reply after hours. The same ads can look like a failure or a success depending on how fast leads are contacted.

sections.h2: Track leads all the way to booked jobs
paragraphs: Install the Meta Pixel together with the Conversions API so Meta receives accurate data even with browser privacy restrictions. Then track what happens after the lead: was it contacted, did it book, did it become a customer? When you can tell Meta which leads turned into real business, campaigns optimize toward quality instead of just volume.

sections.h2: Mistakes to avoid
paragraphs: These are the issues we see most often in service business accounts:
bullets: Generic ads with no offer and no reason to act now
Instant forms with no qualifying questions
Leads sitting in a spreadsheet for a day before anyone calls
Running the same creative for months until performance fades
Judging the channel only on cost per lead instead of cost per booked job

sections.h2: Getting started
paragraphs: Pick one service with a clear offer, create a few simple, authentic ads, choose a lead capture method your team can follow up on quickly and track leads through to booked jobs. Once you know what a customer from Meta costs you, scaling becomes a business decision instead of a guess. If you want help building that system, book a free call with RevUp.

title: Google Business Profile Guide for Local Service Businesses | RevUp
description: How local service businesses in the US can optimize their Google Business Profile to show up in Google Maps and the local map pack: categories, services, reviews and more.
h1: Google Business Profile: how local service businesses win on Google Maps
excerpt: Categories, service areas, reviews and the everyday habits that help plumbers, clinics, contractors and other local service businesses appear in Google Maps and the map pack.

sections.h2: Why your Google Business Profile matters so much
paragraphs: When someone searches for a local service — "dentist near me", "roof repair", "personal injury lawyer" — Google often shows a map with a few businesses before the regular results. Those businesses get calls, direction requests and website visits without paying for a click. Your Google Business Profile is what decides whether you're in that group.
It's free, and for many local service businesses it's the single most important piece of their online presence. Here's how to make the most of it.

sections.h2: Set it up correctly from the start
paragraphs: If you go to your customers instead of having them come to you — plumbers, cleaners, landscapers, mobile services — set up your profile as a service-area business. You can hide your street address and list the cities or areas you serve instead.
Use your real business name exactly as customers see it. Adding keywords or city names to your business name to rank better goes against Google's guidelines and can get your profile suspended.

sections.h2: Choose the right categories
paragraphs: Your primary category is one of the strongest signals Google uses to decide which searches you appear for. Choose the most specific category that describes your main service — for example, a more specific trade category rather than a generic one when it fits. Then add secondary categories for other services you genuinely offer.

sections.h2: Fill in every detail
paragraphs: Complete profiles give Google and customers more reasons to choose you. Make sure you have:
bullets: Services listed individually, with short descriptions
Accurate hours, including holiday hours
A phone number that's answered, and your website link
A description that explains what you do and where, in plain language
Attributes that apply to you, such as language spoken or online appointments

sections.h2: Add real photos regularly
paragraphs: Photos of your team, vehicles, office and finished work show that you're a real, active business. Skip stock images. Add new photos over time — completed projects are perfect content for service businesses.

sections.h2: Build a steady flow of reviews
paragraphs: Reviews influence both your ranking and whether people call you. The most reliable way to get them is simply to ask every satisfied customer, right after the job, with a direct link to your review form. Reply to every review — thank people for positive ones and respond calmly and helpfully to negative ones.
Never buy reviews, write them yourself or offer rewards in exchange for positive ratings. It violates Google's policies and can lead to reviews being removed or your profile being restricted.

sections.h2: Keep your information consistent everywhere
paragraphs: Your business name, phone number and address or service area should match across your website, your profile, social media and directories like Yelp, the BBB and industry sites. Consistent information helps Google trust that your business details are accurate.

sections.h2: Post updates and measure results
paragraphs: Use profile updates to share offers, seasonal services and recent projects. In your profile's performance section you can see how many people called, requested directions or clicked to your website. Add tracking parameters to your website link so visits from your profile show up clearly in Google Analytics.
If you also run Google Ads, link your profile to your ads account so your address and map information can appear in your ads through location assets.

sections.h2: Common mistakes
paragraphs: Watch out for these:
bullets: Keyword-stuffed business names
Using a virtual office or mailbox as a physical address
Leaving categories, services or hours incomplete
Ignoring reviews or only replying to good ones
Letting the profile go months without updates or new photos

sections.h2: Next steps
paragraphs: A well-managed Google Business Profile, a fast website and targeted local ads work best together: the profile builds trust, the website converts and the ads bring volume when you want to grow faster. If you'd like help optimizing your profile or building the rest of the system, book a free call with RevUp.
